title: EITC expansions increased maternal work while reducing some time with children
source_unit: U.S. mothers observed in American Time Use Surveys across EITC expansions since 2003

observations.period: EITC expansions since 2003; working paper issued August 2020 and revised January 2021

denominator.unit: study design and American Time Use Survey analysis; abstract does not state one pooled respondent denominator

eitc_effect_on_maternal_work.unit: reported direction of EITC effect on maternal work

eitc_effect_on_home_production_and_leisu.unit: reported direction of EITC effect on time devoted to home production and leisure

eitc_effect_on_time_with_children.unit: reported direction of EITC effect on time spent with children

active_investment_time.value: almost none of the reduction in time with children came from active investment-related activities

heterogeneity.value: effects concentrated among socioeconomically disadvantaged mothers, especially unmarried mothers and mothers of young children

observations.method: NBER Working Paper 27717 uses American Time Use Surveys to study time allocation around EITC expansions since 2003, with attention to work, home production, leisure, and time with children.
observations.uncertainty: This record retains the official abstract-level directional findings rather than reproduced coefficients, sample construction, or full robustness results. The abstract does not establish a single household's exact schedule, childcare substitute, material recovery, or later political response.
observations.subgroup: U.S. mothers, with reported concentration among socioeconomically disadvantaged mothers, especially unmarried mothers and mothers of young children.
observations.counterinterpretation: The EITC may increase income while also changing work schedules, childcare needs, benefit interactions, and the composition of time. A reduction in total time with children is not equivalent to a reduction in developmental or active-learning time, which the abstract says accounts for almost none of the reduction.

related_sources.claim: NBER DOI and working-paper metadata identify the study and authors Jacob Bastian and Lance Lochner.
Official NBER PDF contains the working-paper abstract and revision metadata.

boundary: This is a U.S. policy-induced time-allocation mechanism, not a universal employment effect or a complete care ledger. It does not identify the exact household's childcare alternative, employer, remedy, civic response, source environment, or political switching/exit.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official NBER Working Paper 27717 page downloaded and hashed; title, date, data source, directional findings, subgroup pattern, and active-investment qualification checked against the abstract.
